answer.sourceLine: This one is Palmer writing about himself, and the citation is unusually specific. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ attributes it to Arnold Palmer: Memories, Stories, and Memorabilia from a Life on and Off the Course (2004), giving p. 52 and ISBN 1584793309. That edition is real: the Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗ matches the same ISBN for a 2004 Stewart, Tabori & Chang printing in New York, and Google Books lists the title under Harry N. Abrams for the same year. What we could not do is read p. 52 — the scan is lending-restricted and Google Books returns no snippet — so the page number above is reported as Wikiquote’s citation rather than as something we confirmed in the book. A search of Quote Investigator returns no article on this line.

source.excerpt: I’ve always believed the British Open is one of the greatest championships in the world. As a kid I read about Bob Jones and Walter Hagen and other Americans who had won the British Open (or Open Championship, as they call it in Britain), and I remember the hero’s welcome Ben Hogan received after returning home with the Claret Jug in 1953.
trail: Wikiquote’s Arnold Palmer page ↗ carries the passage in its sourced quotations with a full book citation — title, publisher, year, ISBN and page 52 — which is a stronger citation than most quotation sites manage. That is the anchor for this record.

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗ independently confirms the book behind that citation, and on the detail that matters for identifying an edition: the ISBN matches Wikiquote’s exactly (1584793309), for a 2004 New York printing of Arnold Palmer: Memories, Stories, and Memorabilia from a Life on and Off the Course.

The text itself we could not reach. The Internet Archive scan is lending-restricted, and the Google Books volume returns no snippet for a search inside it — it reports only that four pages in the book match the word “claret,” which is consistent with a passage mentioning the Claret Jug but is not the sentence. So this record stops at attributed and does not claim page-level confirmation.

Wikipedia’s article on Palmer ↗ supports the context the passage assumes: he travelled to Scotland in 1960 to play the Open Championship for the first time and won it in 1961 and 1962, and that 1960 appearance “drew American attention to the Open Championship, which had previously been ignored by the American golfers.”
source.cutTag: The fuller passage as Wikiquote transcribes it from p. 52
source.excerptNote: The sentence people quote is the opening of a longer passage, and the rest of it explains the sentiment rather than just asserting it: Palmer is tracing his own regard for the championship back to reading about Jones, Hagen and Hogan as a boy. This is Wikiquote’s transcription, not our reading of the page.

author.bio: Arnold Daniel Palmer was an American professional golfer who won 62 PGA Tour titles between 1955 and 1973, including seven major championships, and was among the inaugural inductees into the World Golf Hall of Fame in 1974. The son of a club professional in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, he arrived as television did, and his aggressive, visibly fallible style brought a mass audience to a game that had not had one — his following was known as Arnie’s Army. He also wrote and co-wrote a series of books about the game, this one among the later.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Coming from Palmer, this is not a bland compliment — it is close to a statement of intent. Wikipedia records that before he travelled to Scotland in 1960 to play the championship for the first time, the Open had “previously been ignored by the American golfers.” He went, won it in 1961 and 1962, and the American absence ended with him.

The rest of the passage shows where the regard came from. He credits reading about Bobby Jones and Walter Hagen, and the hero’s welcome Ben Hogan got for bringing home the Claret Jug in 1953 — so the belief predates his own wins by decades. He treated the championship as great before he had any stake in it being great.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote’s sourced section attributes the passage to Arnold Palmer: Memories, Stories, and Memorabilia from a Life on and Off the Course (2004), ISBN 1584793309, p. 52, and transcribes the fuller passage including the Bob Jones, Walter Hagen and Ben Hogan sentences.

The Internet Archive catalogue record confirms a 2004 New York edition of that book with the same ISBN 1584793309. The scan is lending-restricted, so the wording on p. 52 was NOT confirmed in the book text.

Arnold Palmer (1929–2016) won 62 PGA Tour titles from 1955 to 1973 and seven majors; he first played the Open Championship in 1960 and won it in 1961 and 1962, and that 1960 appearance "drew American attention to the Open Championship, which had previously been ignored by the American golfers."
